title: Wind energy development: Examining the potential impact to big game

## Wind Energy Development:

## Examining the Potential Impact to Big Game

## **Amy M. Anderson**

**6/29/2010**

Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University Master of Natural Resources Major:  Natural Resources

Graduate Committee and Approval: Dr. Michael Mortimer (Chair), Dr. David Trauger, Dr. David Robertson

Keywords:  Wind, Wind Energy, Energy Development, Big Game, Impact

## **Table of Contents**

## **ABSTRACT**

Emphasis on the development of renewable energy is being driven by the reality that carbon-based energy sources are polluting the environment and contributing to global warming. This push for alternative energy sources is now fueling the rapid development of wind energy farms, making it the fastest growing source of renewable energy in the world.  This is under the assumption that this renewable source of energy has little or no negative environmental impacts on many facets of wildlife.  In opposition of this assumption, accumulating evidence is available indicating that both policy makers and scientists have misjudged many of the environmental costs entailed on terrestrial wildlife and their habitat.  With the majority of the focus being on avian and bat species, it could be argued that wildlife, big game in particular, are not being monitored and evaluated with as much attention, yet are still suffering considerable effects from development.  With the lack of scientific studies relating to wind energy development and impact on big game, the objective of this paper is to illuminate the readily available evidence relating to other forms of energy development, and parallel it to wind energy development.  By revealing the similarities between the different forms of energy development, it is theorized that the available scientific studies could be utilized to the benefit of big game and their habitat.  These studies clearly illustrate both a direct and indirect impact on big game, and an urgent need for better informed land-use decisions and effective monitoring programs prior to moving forward with wind energy development.

## **INTRODUCTION**

Wind power is one of the fastest growing sources of electricity worldwide (Brown et al. 2007), and for good reason.  It is a renewable indigenous energy source that does not pollute or contribute to global warming.  To fully comprehend these benefits is to also understand that wind energy is an obvious resource that is going to be actively pursued into the future.  Technological advances have helped pushed wind energy into the lead as a resource, and are only going to continue to improve with time (Brown et al. 2007).  This gives this renewable resource the potential to become more cost competitive and popular.

Supporting these advances, wind energy provides a means of meeting the rising political demands for alternative energy sources.  With the renewable energy policies and regulations recently presented as part of the economic stimulus package, an even bigger push to develop and construct wind energy farms is evident.  With the endorsement and promotion of wind energy development, some infer that the inconsistencies and lack of guidance for wind energy comes at a substantial and wide-ranging environmental cost.

Numerous sources agree that much work remains before scientists have a clear understanding of the true impacts to wildlife from wind power (Kuvlesky et al. 2007, GAO 2005a, ASM 2008, Arnett et al. 2007, National Wind Watch 2010, WGFD 2010, WMI 2010). Scientists are particularly concerned about the potential cumulative impacts of wind farms on species populations if the industry expands as expected (GAO 2005a), due to the fact that

scientific knowledge on the effects of wind farms on wildlife populations is scarce (Kuvlesky et al. 2007, Arnett et al. 2007, WGFD 2010).  Part of this trepidation stems from the consideration that these issues should be addressed and resolved prior to development; however, the extent of such cumulative impacts is what continues to remain unclear, including the short- and long-term

trade-offs and costs.  The uncertainty faced by the stakeholders seems to preclude and forestall any clear solutions.  Concerns are further compounded by the fact that the regulation of wind power varies from state-to-state.  State and local regulatory agencies generally have little experience or expertise in addressing environmental and wildlife impacts from wind power (GAO 2005a).

The objective of this paper is to explore the potential current and future impacts of wind energy development on the direct and indirect habitat of big game.  Three ungulate species are the focus, since they occupy a great deal of the environment in which wind farms are placed: mule deer ( _Odocoileus hemionus_ ), pronghorn ( _Antilocapra Americana_ ), and elk ( _Cervus elaphus_ ).  Since there is negligible data relating to big game and wind energy development, scientific studies that have been completed for other energy industries, such as oil and gas, will be explored and related to the field of wind energy development, in an effort to understand the relationship between ungulates and energy development.

It is hypothesized in this paper that if there is any impact to big game as a result of oil and gas development, those impacts could be similar to the development of other energy sources, providing an abundance of scientific studies to be used as a baseline for wind energy

development.  Since oil and gas industry has a proven track record, there are numerous scientific studies demonstrating the relationship between energy development and impact to habitat selection patterns and distribution of mule deer, elk, and pronghorn antelope.  It is inferred that

the same type of habitat fragmentation and impact, to big game that inhabits these environments will also occur with wind energy development.  This data will be used as a basis of exploration to weigh both sides of the issue of wind energy development and its potential associated impact, providing a management framework in which to work.

## **OVERVIEW OF WIND ENERGY**

To set a foundation for the use of wind as a resource, it should be understood that wind is

a converted form of solar energy, and when captured by wind turbines, is a means to transform kinetic energy into a kind of mechanical or electric energy that can be harnessed for use (AWEA 2009).  According to the U.S. Department of Energy wind has historically been used as a source of energy in some form or other, and is recorded as far back as 5000 B.C. as being used to propel boats along the Nile River (2009).  By 200 B.C., simple windmills were being used in China for pumping water, while around the same time the Persians were using vertical axis windmills with woven reed sails to grind their grain (DOE 2009).  Food production was the main use of

windmills, until the Dutch realized their use for draining lakes and marshes in the Rhine River Delta around the 11[th] century.  This same technology was also used in the late 19[th] century, as people moved to the New World, but as the Industrial Revolution started to work its way into the picture, the use of windmills slowly declined (Karnoe 1999).

Use and modernization of windmills during the 19[th] century came as they were used to generate electricity, at which time they became larger in size and started being referred to as ―turbines‖ (DOE 2009).  From a more current perspective, turbines are a recognized source of wind energy as a means of electricity production.  It was estimated that wind turbines were

producing only around three gigawatts (GW or one billion watts) globally around 1993 (Council 2007), which grew to over 59 GW by 2005 (GWEC 2005).

Currently, the United States can generate more than 25,000 MW of electricity from the wind, which is enough to power about 7 million average American homes (NREL 2009).  As of March 2009, renewable energy was said to supply approximately 2.3% of our nation’s energy

with wind energy alone supplying approximately 1.5% of that amount (Stone 2009).  Despite the new administration’s energy policy for 20% renewable energy by the year 2030 (Obama Administration 2008), the U.S. Energy Information Agency (EIA) of the U.S. Department of Energy sees very little change between now and 2030 in the sources of our energy:  around 7% more from coal; 5.5% less from nuclear fission; 1% less from oil; 0.5% less from natural gas; and 0.5% more from renewable sources (2007).  The contribution from wind power is projected to rise from 0.4% to 1.2%, if current incentives and subsidies remain in place (National Wind Watch 2010).  The EIA, however, predicts that the wind’s share of energy production will be less than 1% in 2030 (IEA 2007).  The Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC) forecasts wind-energy generating capacity to continue to grow, reaching 134.8 GW (gigawatts) by the year 2010, with the strongest growth stemming specifically from the United States (2005).

## **WIND POWER SPECS**

To understand both the benefits and impacts that are derived from wind energy, it is important to understand the infrastructure and associated activity and construction that must occur.  As for the specifications of the individual turbines, there are many makes and models as technology continues to change.  One of the more common turbines is the 1.5 MW (megawatt) turbine developed by General Electric (GE).  From the base to the tip of its rotor, the turbine is 380 feet tall with each rotor blade being 122 feet long (Thompson 2009).  Each turbine, weighing around 150 to 350 tons (AWEO 2010, Rosenbloom and Roberson 2007), requires 6 to 8 semi

trucks to transport it to the construction site (Thompson 2009).  The blades sweep a vertical air space of between 1.5 to 2 acres (AWEO 2010, Rosenbloom and Roberson 2007, Rosenbloom 2006).  Each turbine requires acres of clearance for the buried platform of steel-reinforced

concrete, ranging anywhere from 30 to 110 feet deep (Rosenbloom 2006, Rosenbloom and Roberson 2007).

The output of a wind turbine depends upon the wind’s speed and the rotor, but can have power ratings between 250 W (watts) to 5 MW (AWEA 2009).  To provide a reference for the ―watt‖ terminology, the average household consumes approximately 10,000 KW (kilowatts) of electricity each year, while a 10 KW wind turbine can generate around 10,000 KW annually at a site where the wind speeds average 12 miles per hour (AWEA 2009).  An important point to note is that homes only account for one third of electricity use in the United States, and this use varies greatly from day to day, week to week (Rosenbloom 2006).

The plate capacity or the ―capacity factor‖ of an average 1.5 MW is the actual output over a period of time as a proportion of a wind turbine’s maximum capacity, which would be the equivalent of 13,140 MW per year.  The significance of plate capacity is to fully understand that the production of each turbine is not as substantial as the labeled 1.5 MW, providing a foundation to accurately and subjectively weigh the pros and cons of wind energy.

Industry estimates that the majority of the power generated is required by the turbine itself for operation (National Wind Watch 2010), and only around 20% to 29% of the production of a 1.5 MW/h turbine is actually passed onto the transmission lines (Argotsinger 2010,

Rosenbloom 2006).  Combine this with other factors, such as variation of wind speed, volatility, duration, temperature, humidity, wind sheer, and typical efficiency is rated around 30% to 40% of the 3,810.6 MW/year (Argotsinger 2010).  Taking an average of 35% of the 3,810.6 MW/year, it leaves only 1,333.7 MW/year that goes towards production (Argotsinger 2010), meaning, realistically, a turbine can contribute 0.96 MW/h to the transmission grid in the best

conditions.  The average capacity factor for the 137 U.S. wind projects reporting to the Energy Information Agency in 2003 was 26.9% (National Wind Watch 2010).

Wind farms are placed according to the wind class that is determined in certain areas through the use of testing with MET towers (Argotsinger 2010).  Projects must be sited within areas with both sufficient prevailing wind speed to power turbines and access to a transmission grid.  Turbines generate electricity when the wind is between 8 and 55 mph (miles per hour), if they are not shut down for maintenance or repair (National Wind Watch 2010).  If the wind is below 30 mph, the amount of energy generate is very small, meaning a turbine’s average rate of energy production is only around 40% of the time.  The other 60% of the time, the turbine is producing negligible or no energy (National Wind Watch 2010).  As averages go, the fact remains that even windy sites experience intervals of static time, in which the turbines are not generating energy, while on the opposite end of the spectrum, when the wind is too fast, the turbines shut down (Rosenbloom 2006)..

Wind is separated into seven different classifications, according to the speed of the wind. A typical ―cut-in‖ speed is 7 to 9 mph, while a ―cut-out‖ speed is 55 mph (National Wind Watch 2010).  The classes are divided up accordingly:

Wind speed increases 10% between a 150 foot tower and a 300 foot tower, providing 34% more power (Argotsinger 2010).  Typical blade speed of a turbine with 50 foot blades is around 20 to 30 rpm (revolutions per minute) with the tip speed spinning at 180 to 200 rpms (Argotsinger 2010).  When the tip speed accelerates to 200 rpms the turbine shuts down because of aerodynamic factors, such as sound, frost, ice, etc.  At 4 to 8 miles per hour (mph) the turbines start generating power, with 33 mph providing peak production, and 65 mph being the maximum operating speed.  Above 65 mph the blades are turned into the wind with pitch control, which is referred to as ―feathering the blades,‖ and the turbine shuts down (Argotsinger 2010).  For every halving of the wind speed, production of energy drops off by a factor of eight.

The energy created by each turbine, as it is generated, is converted and transferred to the transmission grids, according to priority.  There are three tiers in the power grid:  Tier 1 is meant

for coal, hydropower, and nuclear power; Tier 2 is for natural gas; and Tier 3 is for all renewable energy sources (i.e., wind, solar, geothermal) (Argotsinger 2010).  If the demands for energy are being met, the other tiers are shut down according to priority, with Tier 1 having the top priority. This also has to do with the transmission grids themselves because if they do not have the capacity or are bottlenecking somewhere along the line, then the other tiers are shut down regardless of their production.  Tier 3 with wind power takes last priority, and, therefore, is outweighed by the non-renewable sources of energy.

Without accounting for an increase in energy demand over time, over 100,000 1.5 MW turbines would be required to meet the Department of Energy’s (DOE) goal of only 5% of the United State’s electricity demands from wind energy by the year 2010.  In extrapolating these costs to the country as a whole, this would cost somewhere between $150-$300 billion (Rosenbloom 2006).

## **REGULATIONS AND LAWS – ROLES OF AGENCIES**

With the political call for renewable energy in 2008 (Obama 2008) comes new regulations and laws, along with the distribution of roles and responsibilities for a number of the federal and state agencies.  The federal role in regulating wind power development is limited to projects that either occurs on federal lands or those that have some form of federal involvement, such as projects that receive federal funding (GAO 2005a).  In these cases, wind power projects must comply with federal laws, as well as any relevant state and local laws (GAO 2005a).

Regulating wind power facilities on nonfederal land is largely the responsibility of state and local governments.  While the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission regulates the interstate transmission of electricity, natural gas, and oil, it does not approve the physical construction of electric generation, transmission, or distribution facilities.  This approval is left for state and local governments (GAO 2005a).  In some states, one or more state agencies play a role in regulating wind power development, such as natural resource and environmental

protection agencies, state historic preservation offices, industrial development and regulation agencies, public utility commissions, or siting boards (GAO 2005a).

Several federal policies provide directives and guidance to federal agencies and

developers of wind projects.  On May 18, 2001, the Executive Order 13212 ― _Actions Concerning_

_Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use_ ‖ was created to direct federal agencies involved in reviewing energy-related projects, in an attempt to streamline their internal approval processes (AWEA 2008).  The Energy Policy Act of 2005 and the National Energy Policy of 2001 report provide additional guidance to federal agencies and developers to promote the development of domestic renewable energy supplies (AWEA 2008).  Interagency

working groups, such as _The Federal Interagency Wind Siting Collaboration,_ have evolved out of such national initiatives.  These were created to assist in the coordination between the federal agencies specifically aimed towards wind energy development, and to develop a federal agency wind energy information center (AWEA 2008).

In carrying out the general federal policy regarding wind energy development, federal agencies must review potential impacts from the construction and operation of a wind project, just as they would with any development project (AWEA 2008).  There are numerous federal permitting requirements for wind energy projects, which includes the following:

_National Environmental Policy Act (42 USC 4321); Endangered Species Act (16 USC 1531-1544); Migratory Bird Treaty Act (16 USC 703-712); Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (16 USC 668-668d); National Historic Preservation Act (16 USC 470); Clean Water Act (33 USC 1251 et seq) Section 404 (33 USC 1344); Rivers and Harbors Act of 1899 (33 USC 401 et seq) Section 10 (33 USC 403); Federal Aviation_

_Administration (49 USC 44718); Oil Pollution Act (33 USC 2701 et seq); Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA or Superfund) (42 USC 9601-9675)._

For the framework of this paper, only the first two laws will be touched upon to provide a basis for the regulatory authorities involved and the permitting approval process.  These laws are

the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, both of which pertain to big game and the impact that development of wind farms may have on big game and their habitat.

## **National Environmental Policy Act**

Most important to the discussion of big game is the National Environmental Policy Act, originally signed into law on January 1, 1970 (NEPA) (42 USC 4321), which was the first major environmental law in the United States (NEPAnet 2010).  This important statute requires

agencies to undertake an assessment of the environmental effects of their proposed actions prior to making decisions.  These regulations were promulgated by the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) (40 CFR Parts 1500 – 1508), implementing the procedural provisions of NEPA with each federal agency having its own set of regulations to implement the CEQ’s NEPA regulations (AWEA 2008).

The extent of the environmental assessment necessary during a NEPA review varies based on the significance of the potential impacts associated with a project.  For wind projects that are not located on federal lands, comprehensive environmental reviews most often occur as part of state or local permitting processes, as opposed to part of a federal agency NEPA review (AWEA 2008).  Although federal reviews for wind projects generally consist of consultations or permits that do not require the preparation of lengthy environmental assessment documents, there are a number of activities that may trigger a comprehensive NEPA review (AWEA 2008).

For the purposes of NEPA review, federal agency actions are divided into the three categories:  Categorical Exclusion (CX), Environmental Assessment (EA), and Environmental

Impact Statement (EIS).  When performing NEPA review, the agency must determine which of the categories applies.

## **The Endangered Species Act**

The second law that applies to this topic is the Endangered Species Act (ESA) (16 USC §§ 1531 – 1544), which establishes measures to prevent the extinction of fish, wildlife, and plant species (FWS 1973).  The intention of the ESA is ―to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved‖ and ―to provide a program for the conservation of such species.‖ (ESA §2(b)) (Wikipedia 2010).  The land-based provisions of the ESA are implemented and enforced under regulations promulgated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) (50 CFR Parts 13 and 17) (AWEA 2008), who is responsible for all terrestrial organisms.  The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service administers the ESA as it applies to both private and public entities, however, state wildlife agencies play a cooperative role in the listing and management of threatened and endangered species.

Several principal aspects of wind energy project development, including site clearing and wind turbine operation, may trigger the regulatory requirements of the ESA (AWEA 2008), but is subject to whether the area is regarded as ―critical habitat.‖  Critical habitat includes areas that

have deemed important for the species' survival or recovery and which need special management (FWS 1973).   The federal government is required to use the ―best available scientific information‖ in making a decision about critical habitat (GAO 2005b).  Important to note,

however, is the fact that an agency can also consider economics when deciding what areas should be designated as critical habitat, although it does not consider economic impacts when it "lists" a species (GAO 2005b).

It is through the NEPA process that the FWS plays their role in examining any issues regarding ESA.  FWS is required by the ESA to assist other federal agencies in making certain that any action authorized or put into practice will not endanger any federally listed species. FWS personnel may become involved in the review of potential wind energy development on public lands through NEPA review, involving sections 1501.6 ( _opportunity as a cooperating agency_ ) and section 1503.4 ( _duty to comment on federally-licensed activities for agencies with jurisdiction by law_ ) (FWS 2003b).

## **FWS Interim Guidelines**

Even though U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) does not generally have a direct role in determining whether and how wind power facilities are permitted, they have been involved for roughly twenty years with the wind power industry to help avoid and minimize impacts to wildlife from wind power development (GAO 2005a).  The agency is guided by the Fish and Wildlife Service Mitigation Policy in the Federal Register 46(15) dated from January 1981, which is based around the evaluation of modifications to or loss of habitat caused by development (FWS 2003b).

As of July 2003, the FWS issued ― _Interim Guidelines to Avoid and Minimize Wildlife Impacts from Wind Turbines_ .‖  These guidelines stem from the FWS’ belief that as more facilities with larger turbines are constructed, the cumulative effects may contribute to the decline of wildlife populations (FWS 2003b).  The intent of such is to assist the wind energy industry in avoiding or minimizing impacts to wildlife and their habitats (FWS 2003b).  The purpose of these guidelines was to be produced with the best available science, with the understanding that they would be updated as new information becomes available (FWS 2010).

A very important point to note, however, is that these _Guidelines_ are only voluntary interim guidelines, and are not mandatory in federal agency land use plan decisions (FWS 2003b).  Such is stated in the memorandum coming from the Department of Interior (DOI) that came out two months prior to the Guidelines.

_... the wind industry is rapidly expanding into habitats and regions that have not been well studied. The Service therefore suggests a precautionary approach to site selection and development and will employ this approach in making recommendations and assessing impacts of wind-energy developments. We encourage the wind-energy industry to follow these guidelines and, in cooperation with the Service, to conduct scientific research to provide additional information on the impacts of wind-energy development on wildlife.  We further encourage the industry to look for opportunities to promote bird and other wildlife conservation when planning wind-energy facilities (e.g., voluntary habitat acquisition or conservation easements)_ (FWS 2003b) _._

Until the Secretary of Interior determines the applicability of final guidelines for the Department of Interior agencies, the FWS interim guidelines are only used as a general guide to assist the BLM in siting decisions and the design of pre-development surveys, mitigation measures, and post-construction monitoring for site-specific projects (GAO 2005a).

On December 8, 2003, the American Wind Energy Association (AWEA) submitted comments on the Interim Guidelines to the FWS.  AWEA noted that the lack of consultation

with the wind industry prior to issuance of the guidance had ―resulted in a document that has technical flaws, contains inaccurate assumptions, and calls for a level of regulation

disproportionate to wind’s impacts on wildlife, especially as compared to impacts from other activities (AWEA 2008).

According to AWEA (2008), on April 26, 2004, the FWS issued a memorandum regarding implementation of the Interim Guidelines.  Among other things, the FWS clarified that the guidance is intended to be general in nature and should be applied as appropriate based on local conditions. The FWS stated that the ―Interim Guidelines are not to be construed as rigid requirements, which are applicable to every situation, nor should they be read literally‖ (AWEA 2008).  The Memorandum from the DOI also stated that _“[F]ield offices have discretion in the use of these guidelines on a case-by-case basis, and may also have additional recommendations to add which are specific to their geographic area_ ‖ (FWS 2003a).  Regardless of these statements, federal and state agencies, in addition to other stakeholders, continue to apply the Interim Guidelines as mandatory requirements, without taking into consideration site-specific considerations (WGA 2008).

According to AWEA’s Siting Handbook, on March 13, 2007, DOI announced the formation of a Wind Turbine Guidelines Federal Advisory Committee (FACA) to provide recommendations and advice to the DOI and the FWS ―on developing effective measures to protect wildlife resources and enhance potential benefits to wildlife that may be identified‖ (2008).  The FACA presented a critical opportunity for the FWS to publish a revised document that is protective of wildlife, yet no update or additional guidelines have yet been published.  In fact, it wasn’t until March of 2010 that a different approach was examined.  In the original Guidelines, ten ―research needs on the impacts of wind power development on wildlife‖ were identified and suggested.  The majority of the research needs mentioned are related directly to avian and bat mortality, while only one mentioned that of big game:  Localized effects of turbines on wildlife:  habitat fragmentation and loss; effects of noise on both aquatic and terrestrial wildlife; habituation.

## **SITING GUIDELINES**

The regulatory process for siting a wind energy project varies widely from state to state (AWEA 2008).  For example, some states have vested primary siting authority in a state agency while others have left this authority to local governments to handle through their land use and zoning ordinances (AWEA 2008).  This brings to light the fact that there is great diversity among state programs and no consistency in the proper procedure or guidelines.

Prior to commencing a wind energy project in any state, a developer should determine the applicable regulatory structure and understand the allocation of responsibility among federal, state, and local government agencies (AWEA 2008).  The lack of uniformity among regulatory programs means that what may be a simple, streamlined review process before a single agency in one state may be a complex, time-consuming process involving multiple levels of review in another state (AWEA 2008).

The factors for siting for the turbines and their associated transmission lines have become extremely scrutinized, mainly due to the lack of consistency and regulation, proving that the measures for calculating environmental impacts are still being fine-tuned.  Numerous cases filed in federal courts pertaining to siting issues, alleging violations of federal law, have created disparate precedents because of deference to local law issues (Stone 2009).  If wind farm siting litigation continues on its current path of division, the courts are unlikely to ever offer wind farm developers uniform guidance (Stone 2009).

With wind farm siting comes the short and long term factors of impact that must be addressed.  This includes taking into account erosion, disruption of water flow and soil

composition, destruction of habitat and vegetation, in addition to the access roads, transmission

lines, transformers, and the turbine sites themselves.  Construction requires heavy equipment, involving bulldozers, graders, trenching machines, concrete trucks, flatbed trucks, and large cranes.  Construction of the access roads requires wide straight compacted roads for the transportation of the turbine housings (56 tons) and blade assemblies (36 tons) (Rosenbloom 2006).

A site needs at least 15 to 20 turbines to make an investment in the required transmission infrastructure worthwhile (Rosenbloom 2006).  Each tower requires 5 to 10 times the rotor diameter from neighboring towers or trees for optimal performance (Rosenbloom 2006).  This means that for every tower with 115 foot rotors, a quarter to half of a mile is required as a radius. Some examples used by Rosenbloom (2006) states that a facility in Scotland represents 50 acres for each MW of rated capacity, while in the United States FPL Energy asserts they require 40 acres per installed MW and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) maintains 60 acres is more likely.  Worldwide, facilities commonly use 30 to 70 acres per MW, which means 120 to 280 acres for every MW of ―likely average output‖ at 25% capacity factor (Rosenbloom 2006).

In line with the administration’s call for the use of renewable energy, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) prepared a technical report in May 2008 titled _20% Wind Energy by 2030:  Increasing Wind Energy's Contribution to U.S. Electricity Supply_ .  The report examines siting issues and effects that an increase in wind power facilities may have on compatible land uses, water use, aesthetics, and wildlife habitats.  One of the major challenges that came up in the _20% Wind_ scenario path included addressing potential concerns about local siting, wildlife, and environmental issues (DOE 2008).  This expressed concern is shared by many, demonstrating there is still much lacking in the way of a reliable structure of guidelines

for the protection of wildlife and siting issues overall (DOE 2008, Kuvlesky et al. 2007, GAO 2005a, ASM 2008, Arnett et al. 2007, National Wind Watch 2010, WMI 2010).

## **BIG GAME AND ENERGY DEVELOPMENT**

Large, continuous healthy ecosystems that contain native wildlife populations, combined with public access to natural landscapes, contribute to the West’s quality of life and economic security (WGA 2008).  The movement of the wildlife through their natural and learned corridors and into what is considered crucial habitats are critical to maintaining these Western qualities.  A study conducted by the Western Governors’ Association stated that wildlife-associated recreation brings important economic benefits to communities throughout the West.  Small rural communities benefit from the revenue that comes with tourism, hunting and fishing, and other forms of outdoor recreation (WGA 2008), and, in fact, retail tax revenue for many small

communities is provided during the key hunting and fishing seasons.  In the contiguous Western states, more than 43.6 million people participated in hunting, fishing or wildlife watching in 2006, spending almost $33.6 billion (WGA 2008).  Obviously, this revenue solely relies on healthy, reliable wildlife populations, which in turn, depend on native habitat and movement through migratory routes.

It is acknowledged that the integrity of wildlife ecosystems in the West and throughout the United States is at risk due to the development that is occurring in these migration corridors and key habitats (WGA 2008).  Throughout time, people have been drawn to wild places as a means of escaping human industrialism and development, and count on viewing an unspoiled environment or retreat (WGA 2008).

Across the western United States, in particular, energy development placement can compromise wildlife and the environment.  This impact is almost certainly true if the placement is done in a careless manner without the proper guidelines (Kuvlesky et al. 2007).  Over the years, a vast collection of scientific literature and discussion on energy development has demonstrated how the patterns of land use can influence the movement of big game and the functioning of their ecosystems (ASM 2008, GAO 2005a, Hobbs 1989, Johnson et al. 1981, Kuvlesky et al. 2007, NRC 2007, Sawyer 2005, Sawyer et al. 2006, Sawyer et al. 2007, WAFWA 2002, WGA 2008, WGFD 2010, WMI 2010).  When land is converted to human land uses, natural habitat is consumed by a different use, and the remaining habitat is, to differing degrees, altered due to fragmentation and degradation of habitat.  It is surmised in the preceding literature that the extent to which large numbers of wind turbines might impact wildlife is presently unknown and more problematic than most believe, simply because of the lack of scientific data directed towards wind energy development.

Since wind energy farms are a relatively new development, there have not been a large number of wind power facilities in the United States that have been thoroughly studied in terms of big game, especially for long-term impacts.  Direct ungulate habitat loss from wind energy development may be relatively small, since roads and turbines constitute only a small percentage of the area (Strickland 2004); however, it is the indirect habitat loss affecting the use of

ungulates that is so indefinite (WGFD 2010).  Further, much is still unknown about migratory routes and the cumulative impact that the wind power industry may have on wildlife species. Consequently, the potential exists to displace big game species from crucial seasonal habitats and disconnect essential habitat components (WGFD 2010.  Notably, the main focus of study has

been directed towards avian species and bats and ways to reduce the fatalities at wind power facilities (GAO 2005a), rather than big game that use these same areas.

Given the relatively narrow regulatory scope of state and local agencies and lack of mandatory guidelines, it seems that when new wind power facilities are permitted, consideration is not given to the impacts of wind power on an ―ecosystem‖ scale—a scale that often spans governmental jurisdictions (GAO 2005a).  Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), in its responsibility for protecting wildlife on a state level, is the appropriate agency for such a task of monitoring the status of species populations, to the extent possible.  Because the FWS and different state Game and Fish agencies operate at state levels, the difficulty of scale could present itself as an issue. Because wildlife in the U.S. faces a multitude of national threats, FWS officials informed Government Accountability Office (GAO) that it generally spends a small portion of its time assessing the impacts from wind power (GAO 2005a).

It has been stated that the major shortcoming of efforts to evaluate the impacts of disturbances on wildlife populations is that they seldom are addressed in an experimental framework but, rather, tend to be short-term and observational (Sawyer et al. 2006).  Overall, scientific literature on the effects of wind farms on wildlife populations is negligible (Kuvlesky et al. 2007)  Sawyer et al. determined that short, post-development observation and monitoring plans related to the regulatory work generally resulted in little or no information that allowed agencies and industry to assess the full impacts on wildlife (2006).  The ecological influences of wind energy facilities are complex, and vary with spatial and temporal scale, location, season, weather, ecosystem type, species, and other factors (NRC 2007).  Moreover, many of the influences are cumulative, and ecological influences can interact in complex ways.

## **Big Game Habitat**

The three ungulate species that are the focus of this paper rely on different seasonal ranges to meet their annual nutrition and energetic requirements, in addition to shelter (Sawyer et al. 2005, McCullough 1985, Sawyer et al. 2006, Lima 1998, Baker 1978, Grover 1986, Hobbs 1989).  An important point to understand is that because seasonal ranges often occur great distances apart and across a mix of vegetation types and land ownership, maintaining migration corridors to and from these ranges can be difficult, especially if the land managers do not have detailed information on mule deer, elk, and pronghorn movements (Sawyer et al. 2006).

Migration is an adaptive behavioral strategy that allows these ungulate populations to avoid resource shortages in temperate regions (Baker 1978) and find greater food sources prior to breeding (Sinclair 1983).  Migrations between the seasonal ranges generally follow traditional routes that are learned and passed on from mother to young (McCullough 1985).  According to an archaeological study in western Wyoming, evidence suggests migration routes have been used for thousands of years (Miller et al. 1999), providing access to a variety of summer and winter ranges across enormous areas and rugged topography (Sawyer et al. 2005).  The significance of migratory routes is that without them, many of the seasonal ranges would be inaccessible to the ungulate populations.  The ending result of the fragmentation of migratory routes is that it would be unlikely the current populations could be maintained (Saywer et al. 2005).  Therefore, in taking into consideration wind farm development and the conjectured fragmentation that could

occur to the environment, identification and protection of migration routes should be considered an integral part of big game management.  The unknown here, however, lies with the fact that there is no current evidence that undermines or supports the extent of fragmentation of migratory routes in relation to wind farm development.

## **Potential Impact**

Public lands with high gas potential often coincide with regions that support large mule deer populations (Sawyer et al. 2007).  Sawyer reasons that the impacts of natural gas development on mule deer may include the direct loss (i.e., surface disturbance) of habitat from such things as well pads, access road, and pipeline construction.  Indirect habitat losses may occur if increased human activity (i.e., traffic, noise) associated with infrastructure cause mule deer to alter their habitat use patterns (Sawyer et al. 2005).

Impacts that would occur from wind power development would be associated with the footprint (the acreage or area impacted by construction of the wind farm) resulting from construction of turbines as well as infrastructure development, such as the construction of buildings, roads, and electrical transmission lines. Habitat disturbance associated with footprints will be a function of the size and numbers of turbines that are constructed on the development site (Kuvlesky et al. 2007).

While it is relatively easy to quantify the direct habitat losses that result from conversion of native vegetation to infrastructure related to energy development, it is much more difficult to document indirect habitat losses (Saywer et al. 2007, WGFD 2010).  Nonetheless, because indirect impacts may affect a substantially larger area than direct impacts (Sawyer et al. 2007, WGFD 2010), it could be deduced that there is a great need to better understand how development can lead to this indirect habitat loss in the future.  Unfortunately, without current scientific studies to support and quantify if and how wind energy development impacts indirect habitat, there is no basis for such a structure, other than comparing wind energy development to that of other energy development.

A 2007 study of mule deer in Sublette County, home to the largest energy development in the State of Wyoming, performed by Sawyer, Nielson, and Strickland identified three key components for assessing potential impacts to mule deer.  These components include 1) direct habitat loss, 2) indirect habitat loss and 3) population performance (Sawyer et al., 2007).

The first component, direct habitat loss, occurs when native vegetation is converted to any kind of infrastructure (Sawyer et al. 2007).  It can consist of everything from surface disturbance and site preparation activities, movement of large machinery, transportation of turbine elements, to ―feeder lines‖ and transmission lines leading from the wind energy facility to the electricity grid (NRC 2007).  All of these things can lead to removal and disturbance of vegetation, compaction of soil, soil erosion, and change of hydrologic features (NRC 2007).  The impacts can be local and short-term or more indirect and long term, and have a substantial effect on habitat quality for a variety of organisms.

The second component, indirect habitat loss, takes place if or when the mule deer use declines by means of displacement or avoidance in areas adjacent to or near infrastructure (Sawyer et al. 2007).  It deals with the change in habitat selection and migration routes.  The third component included several measures of population performance, which included estimates of mule deer abundance, survival, and recruitment in a specified area (Sawyer et al. 2007).

As part of the study, Sawyer, Nielson, and Strickland used a combination of radio-collars equipped with GPS and statistical analyses to identify mule deer distribution and habitat selection patterns, and then evaluated how or if those patterns were influenced by gas development (2007).  They then used a weight-of-evidence approach that measured an assortment of data collected from both the treatment and reference area to assess how or if mule

deer population performance in the study area was affected by gas development (Sawyer et al. 2007).

The study found that radio-marked deer avoided well pads 6 of the 7 years of

development.  This resulted in indirect habitat loss that was substantially larger than the direct habitat loss (Sawyer et al. 2007).  Mule deer avoidance of well pads was found to be associated with the amount of human activity that occurred at the pads (Sawyer et al. 2007).  Data collected from the study area indicated that mule deer numbers declined during the first four years (20012004), and when the estimated survival and recruitment rates were incorporated into a population growth model, the model predicted a 27% decline (Sawyer et al. 2007) directly due to the energy development.

Pronghorn antelope are also impacted by many of the same disturbances and fragmentation of habitat.  While many of the historic pronghorn ranges are still occupied, herds are much smaller and more isolated (Yoakum and O’Gara 2000).  Habitat loss and movement barriers have contributed to this fragmentation and general decline of pronghorn populations (Yoakum and O’Gara 2004).

The Game and Fish Department of North Dakota state that the greatest impact from energy development and production to pronghorn is that of habitat loss and displacement, which has been the cause of pronghorn movement into bordering habitats (2006).  This increases the use of sub-optimal habitats, conflicts with agriculture, and human confrontations (Game and Fish Department 2006).  Roadways pose a major concern for pronghorn populations, both as a barrier to movements, hindering their movements (Riddle and Oakley 1973), and as a mortality source from vehicle collisions (Yoakum and O’Gara 2004, Van Riper et al 1998).  Increased stress from human activity displaces the pronghorn from their preferred habitats (Game and Fish Department

2006).  The Game and Fish plainly state that energy development has impacted pronghorn habitat in several western states, and the land use practices will continue to significantly alter western rangelands (2006).

St. John performed a study in 1995 in regards to elk and the decrease in activity when a native environment has been fragmented.  He concluded that elk adjusted their foraging behavior by browsing far enough away from roads so as to avoid human contact and possible predation (1995).  His studies illustrated that aspen stands within 500 meters of a road were browsed significantly less than aspen stand farther away (St. John 1995).  Previous studies by Lyon (1979), Rost and Bailey (1979), Ward (1980), and Johnson and Lockman (1981) all provide supportive evidence that elk populations move away from any location that exhibits human activity.

## **HABITAT FRAGMENTATION**

Habitat fragmentation can be defined as the breaking up of large contiguous tracts of suitable habitat for a species into increasingly smaller patches that are isolated from each other by barriers consisting of unsuitable or less suitable habitat (NRC 2007).  The analysis performed in Sublette County, Wyoming suggests that mule deer steer clear of energy development infrastructure, and the avoidance was directly influenced by the level of human activity at the well pads (Sawyer at al. 2007), signifying how fragmentation of a habitat has a significant effect on the behavior of ungulates.

## **Edge Influence**

The National Research Council also discusses a fragmentation issue called the ―depth of edge influence‖ (2007), which is sometimes referred to as the functional edge (Wood et al. 2006).  The creation of an edge in conjunction with fragmentation causes numerous different biological changes (Harper 2005).  This impact is stated to radiate outside of the area actually disturbed by turbine development for some species of a distance up to 100 to 200 meters in all directions from the ―footprint‖ (Freddy et al. 1986, Taylor and Knight 2003).  Wood et al. (2006) states that disruptions can exceed 340 meters in all directions for certain species, or have a habitat impact of more than 24 hectares per MW, assuming a 1.5 MW turbine.  Creation of additional habitat for edge-associated species may place some of these species at higher risk than if the turbines were not present (NRC 2007).

Laverty and Gibbs studied habitat fragmentation and the edge influence that is associated with such and focused the effects down to three elements relating to the formation of an ―edge‖ and biological impact:  (1) invasion by generalist species; (2) alteration of plant communities; and (3) alteration of insect communities and nutrient cycling (Laverty and Gibbs 2006).  All of these things fall back to the biological changes in species composition, abundance, distribution, interaction (i.e., predation, competition, pollination, and seed dispersal) that occurs with the ―edge‖ element.

## **Human Disturbance**

There is great deal of literature that indicates wildlife respond to human disturbances similarly to how they respond to predation risk (Frid and Dill 2002).  For example, the habitat selection patterns of elk are affected by the presence of wolves (Creel et al. 2005, Winnie and

Creel 2007, Creel et al. 2008), which may vary spatially or temporally, but is similar to how the levels of human disturbance may vary across a developed gas, oil, or wind field.  Just like predation risk, human disturbance can redirect crucial time and energy away from survival requirements like foraging and resting, (Frid and Dill 2002), and, therefore, can be important to wintering mule deer, whose energy balance is closely linked to survival (Sawyer et al. 2007). Disturbance, overall, decreases the viability of ungulate subpopulations.

Hungry or malnourished animals are more likely to feed in riskier habitats in order to meet their energetic requirements and avoid starvation, as pointed out by Lima (1998) and Brown and Kotler (2004).  Given the variable nutritional condition of wintering ungulates, it is reasonable to expect those in poor body condition are less likely displaced by perceived risk because the benefit of foraging outweighs the risk of predation. Therefore, during harsh winters when ungulates are in poor body condition and forage availability is reduced, it is possible that they ignore the perceived risk from developed areas in favor of maximizing their foraging opportunities.

Lima and Dill (1990) found mule deer response to well pads, for example, was consistent with predictions of predation risk theory.  The predation risk literature suggests that anti-predator behavior (e.g., fleeing, vigilance, habitat selection) has an energetic cost by reducing time spent in other energy positive activities (e.g., foraging, resting). Accordingly, prey animals must actively balance their foraging requirements with avoiding perceived risk (Lima and Dill 1990).

The relationship between disturbance to a native habitat and energy required by ungulates to alter their routes or move into different surroundings has been studied, demonstrating that there is a definite increase in the energy expenditure required (Parker et al. 1984, Hobbs 1989). The obvious displacement of deer, in these studies, from high-use areas to a low-use area that

display less disturbance definitely has the potential to influence both the reproduction and survival of ungulate populations.

The studies completed by Parker et al (1984) and Hobbs (1989) provides some context for mule deer energetics and flight distances associated with human disturbances.  For example, both Freddy et al. (1986) and Taylor and Knight (2003) reported flight distances of disturbed mule deer ranging from 100 to 200 m.   This distance may seem trivial, however, when one considers mule deer in a study area, such as the one scrutinized by Sawyer et al. in the oil fields in Sublette County, Wyoming, mule deer only move approximately 1,600 meters to 2,300 meters a day during the winter month (Sawyer et al. 2007).  Therefore, a 200 meter disturbance represents 9% to 13% of their daily movement and associated energetic requirements, which can mean a great deal when taking into account the energy required to move through a snowy habitat.

Conclusively, Sawyer et al. and the studies that resulted suggested that the response of mule deer to energy infrastructure was functionally comparable to how prey animals respond to the risk of predation, and that mule deer appeared to perceive the varying levels of risk from the human interference and scaled their behaviors accordingly (2009).  Overall, the studies illustrate the undeniable impact that human activity related to energy development has in these environments, altering the behavior patterns of associated ungulates.  This especially holds true when ungulates are most vulnerable to stress during winter months when they require supplementary energy expenditure for movement and are experiencing reduced foraging opportunities.

## **Roads, Fences, Barriers**

A major contribution to the human influence into these wind farm environments is the road networks that are constructed to service the turbines.  The coverage of road networks depends on the size of the wind farm.  Facilities consisting of several hundred or more turbines will have extensive road networks leading to every individual turbine.  Trombulak and Frissell (2000) reviewed literature relevant to road effects on all terrestrial and aquatic communities, and, based on their analysis, they concluded that the presence of roads is associated with negative effects on biotic integrity and could result in loss of biodiversity at local and regional scales. Their studies included roads of all kinds, and was found to affect terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems in seven different ways:  1) increased mortality from road construction; 2) increased mortality from collision with vehicles; 3) modification of animal behavior; 4) alteration of the physical environment; 5) alteration of the chemical environment; 6) spread of exotic species; and 7) increased alteration and use of habitats by humans (Trombulak and Frissell 2000).  Their conclusion was that, in light of the broad range of ecological effects of roads and associated multiplicity of effects, it is critical to preserve the remaining roadless or near-roadless portions of the landscape (Trombulak and Frissell 2000).

The construction of roads networking their way to every individual turbine and infrastructure leads to numerous and diverse changes in the native environment.  Road transformations can include changes in temperature, soil water content and compaction, light, dust, surface water flow, pattern of run-off, and sedimentation of down-slope aquatic habitats (Helvey and Kochenderfer 1990).  A study prepared in 2009 by Denholm et al. for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), titled _Land-Use Requirements of Modern Wind Power Plants in the United States_ , indicated that the majority of direct impacts to habitat in wind

development are associated with roads.  This demonstrates that the majority of the direct impact in a wind farm stems from the construction and use of roads.  The roads analyzed in the study pertain only to new road development or road improvement in relation to large wind facilities constructed after 2000 (172 individual projects).
